Life rarely turns out the way you plan it

When I was a kid, I thought I had it all figured out:

- Get into a good college.
- Study engineering.
- Get a good job.
- Work for 4–5 years.
And maybe, at 26 or 27, if I felt brave enough, start something of my own.

Somewhere along the way, life had other plans.
- At 15 I found myself interested in tech, building robots and alarm clocks, and gave my first Tedx talk.
- At 17, I closed my first project with Microsoft building AI Agents.
- At 18 I built software for clients from the US, UK, Singapore, Dubai etc, constantly finding myself in industries I knew very little about just a few months earlier.

And somewhere in the middle of all of that i met jeremy zechariah abraham and we started studojo.

Today, I'm 19, working with a team of 10 to build an AI career-tech platform, and we've already helped 350+ job seekers land jobs they once only hoped for.
And now post our demo day at Mesa School of Business, we have received ₹1.6 Cr in soft commitments from investors who believe in what we're building.

It's a strange number to process when you think about where I started. 

If you tell kid Pranav, that people are willing to bet on the ideas of a crazy teenager, he wouldn’t believe you whatsoever.

I don't think that kid would understand half of what we're doing today.

But I think he'd be proud. And maybe that’s all that matters…

We're looking to raise a round of ₹2.5 Cr, so if you're an investor interested in AI, career-tech, employability or the future of work, I'd love to have a conversation. 
And if someone comes to mind who should be part of this journey, I'd be grateful for an introduction.

₹64,00,00,00,000 per annum.

That's apparently what a Summer Analyst intern at Goldman Sachs gets paid.
Or at least that's what the JD says.

Obviously, it's a mistake.

And no, this doesn't make Goldman Sachs any less of a company. One typo in a document doesn't change the quality of its people, culture, or opportunities.

But it did make me think.

If this was a candidate's resume instead of a company's JD, would we be as forgiving?
A wrong capitalization.
An extra space.
A formatting inconsistency.
A typo.

We've somehow reached a point where a one-page document is expected to perfectly represent a person's competence. And if it doesn't, it can be enough to never get a callback.

The irony is that we instinctively know a typo doesn't define Goldman Sachs. Yet we're often willing to let similar mistakes define a candidate.

Maybe the bigger issue isn't that resumes have flaws.
Maybe it's that we've started treating resumes as far stronger indicators of ability than they really are.

With AI making resumes, cover letters, and portfolios easier than ever to generate, I don't think this problem is going away, it'll only get worse.

I'm genuinely curious:

If resumes are becoming weaker signals of talent, what do you think should replace them?
Work samples? Paid trials? Case studies? Something else entirely?

I'd love to hear what founders, recruiters, and hiring managers have found actually predicts great candidates.

We ran a small experiment. (to figure out why your resume sucks!)

We took 2 real resumes from students in our community. 

Same person, same work experience, two different formats.

Version A was a standard template: objective statement at the top, responsibilities listed under each role.
Version B had no objective statement and had results-based bullets in a clean one-pager.

We showed both to 8 hiring managers without telling them they were the same person. (yeah we changed the name)

Version B got 7 out of 8 to say they'd want to speak to the candidate. (he landed interviews just due to this experiment)

Version A got 2 on 8

The experience on the page was identical. We just changed the read.

This matters because the resume is your first impression on the recruiter, make it stand out

this is the email that got a reply from one of India's largest IT companies in 3 days 👀

breaking it down line by line so you can steal the formula

Subject: "Quick question about [Company]'s ed-tech direction"
→ not "internship application." a question. not the same as the 200 other emails in that inbox.

Line 1: "I'm [Name], a 3rd year CS student at [College] — I've been following [Company]'s expansion into adaptive learning and had a quick question about the direction."
→ shows research. shows specificity. doesn't open with "I am seeking a challenging opportunity."

Line 2: "I've built a small adaptive quiz engine as a project, [GitHub link], and I'm curious whether the team experiments with this kind of personalisation on the content side."
→ leads with proof before asking for anything. completely flips the dynamic.

Line 3: "Would love to contribute for a few months if there's a fit, open to a 15-minute call if that works."
→ small ask. low friction. easy to say yes to.

Result: reply from HR in 3 days. interview scheduled.

the formula isn't magic. it's research + proof + a real conversation starter.

But the more time we spent in the ecosystem, the more we realised something:
 
If we want to meaningfully change the student journey, we can't just build for students.
 
There are colleges, companies, educators and organisations working with thousands of students and a lot of them are still using spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups, forms and a collection of disconnected tools to manage it all.
 
And that's where Sensei comes in.
 
Studojo helps students get ahead. Sensei helps the organisations helping them.
 
We're building Sensei as a B2B platform for organisations to engage their student communities, run programs, create opportunities and ultimately help more students become career-ready.
 
And honestly, the last few weeks have looked something like this.
 
A ridiculous number of conversations with colleges, companies, educators and people much smarter than us.
 
A lot of questions, a lot of ideas, and a lot of things we hadn't considered when we first started Studojo.
 
But that's exactly what made us realise there's something here.
 
There are millions of students trying to figure out their careers.
 
And there are thousands of organisations trying to help them do it.

We think both sides deserves better tools 
 
That's what we're building with Sensei. 🥋

every founder says they hire for "ownership" after 200+ conversations with recruiters and hiring managers, we've never once heard one say that's what actually got someone hired

they don't have a word for it. they just remember the moment

"she noticed our onboarding page had a broken link during the interview. fixed the copy herself. didn't ask permission"
 "he followed up after the call with three ideas nobody asked for"
 "two weeks into the internship, she rebuilt a process that had annoyed everyone for a year. never brought it up in a meeting"

none of them said "ownership" all of them told a story

that's the actual pattern. candidates who claim ownership in an interview rarely get remembered. the ones who did something small and unasked for, in the room or right after, are the ones who get the offer

if you're hiring right now: the word is the thing to ignore. the story is the thing to test for. 

and if you're seeking a job: show up prepare, a small 30 min prep goes a long way!

we've watched this pattern from both sides of the table for a while now. it holds every time

after applying to more than 100 internships and hearing back nothing, i decided to solve it

now i'm on the other side of it, helping students land the internships and jobs they actually want.

47,078 emails sent. replies from Bain & Company, Meesho, and VC-backed startups.
every tier we offer is built to get you at least one reply back, we don't stop until you get one

What a Rs.13,000 gym membership taught me about life:

I've tried the gym a bunch of times over the last few years. It always starts with full josh, ready to undergo some sorta evolution in 60 days. And always ends the same (not positive).

However four months ago, I bought an yearly membership for the first time, mainly cuz Cult subscriptions are hilarious for anything lower (must be all the Hrithik Roshan ads).

And the cycle of josh starts again but fortunately this time it didn't stop???

Here's why, I think.

Every other time, the gym was a goal. Brad Pitt in Fight Club by day 60. So every session felt like it mattered too much. Skip one day and I feel like I'm wasting the membership. So I'd go 6 days a week from day 1 and obviously burn out super fast and quit.

This year, that whole pressure just... vanished.

And I think it's cuz one year is SUCH a long time that my brain kinda gave up on the whole "transform by X date" thing. There's no realistic 1 year body goal I could obsess over. So I just stopped. And went, okay, I'll just keep doing the boring stuff, show up, eat decent food, and we'll see where I'm at in a year.

That turned out to be the exact mentality I needed i guess.

Because now a bad week means nothing. When it's a goal, a bad week means the goal is slipping away, i'm behind. When its an identity, now I'm just a guy who goes to the gym who had a bad week. Next week I go again. Nothing broke.

Now apply that to money.

Most of us are secretly running on "rich in the next 6 months" (was me, fully). It doesn't happen on time, so we go "welp, wrong path" and start over. New idea, new hustle, repeat every few months.

But what if you just... zoomed out? Like bro, just build cool stuff for 5 years. Meet nice people, work on things that matter, keep showing up, and we'll see where it goes. 

Nobody who got properly rich started with "get rich in 6 months." They just became someone who builds cool things. The money was the side effect.

Anyway, that's Rs.13,000 worth of gym wisdom for a body I still don't have. But hey, I'm someone who goes to the gym now.

Subject: "Quick question about [Company]'s ed-tech direction"
→ not "internship application." a question. not the same as the 200 other emails in that inbox.

Line 1: "I'm [Name], a 3rd year CS student at [College] — I've been following [Company]'s expansion into adaptive learning and had a quick question about the direction."
→ shows research. shows specificity. doesn't open with "I am seeking a challenging opportunity."

Line 2: "I've built a small adaptive quiz engine as a project, [GitHub link], and I'm curious whether the team experiments with this kind of personalisation on the content side."
→ leads with proof before asking for anything. completely flips the dynamic.

→ small ask. low friction. easy to say yes to.
